newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's helpers confident in future.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's helpers confident in future.

text.p: Sambhu Biswas has worked for 12 years in the slums of Calcutta, a soldier in Mother Teresa's volunteer army combatting poverty and death.
On the day the charismatic nun handed over command of her religious order, Biswas was toiling at Mother Teresa's home for the dying, confident her successor Sister Nirmala would meet the challenge.
"I feel Sister Nirmala will be able to carry on the task," Biswas told Reuters. "She is just like Mother Teresa."
Biswas works at "Nirmal Hriday" (Sacred Heart), located near a Hindu temple and surrounded by slums, treating diseased persons picked up from the streets of his home city Calcutta and its suburbs.
He said 90 patients were receiving care in the home.
Mother Teresa, ever ready despite her 86 years to recruit new helpers, told journalists at a news conference on Friday: "Kindly go to the dying and destitute and give tender love to them."
Biswas's confidence in Sister Nirmala's abilities was echoed by nuns and other volunteers who in Mother Teresa's image devote their lives to the destitute.
"We are very happy and confident that she will carry forward Mother's spirit and work," said a nun, who asked not to be identified. "With Mother's guidance, she will do well."

Sister Nirmala took command of the 49-year-old Missionaries of Charity order after winning a drawn-out election for a successor to the gritty but ailing Mother Teresa, who has become a byword for selflessness and is called "Saint of the Gutters".

"Mother is like a God," said Heera (Eds: one name), a tuberculosis patient who was brought to Sacred Heart three months ago. "I had no money to be treated at a hospital and was brought here for treatment. Sisters take care of us very well."
Mother Teresa and Sister Nirmala joined other nuns in morning prayers on Friday at 6 a.m. (0030 GMT) in the chapel inside Mother House, the order's headquarters.
Visitors were not allowed to attend.
Michael Gomes walked slowly out of Mother House after attending morning prayers. The Missionaries of Charity began operations in Gomes's Calcutta home in its early years.
"Excellent," he said when asked about Sister Nirmala's election. "She (Sister Nirmala) has certain norms which everyone else doesn't have."
A Hindu Brahmin who converted to Roman Catholicism at age 23, Sister Nirmala opened the Missionaries of Charity's first home outside India and has led the order's contemplative wing for 28 years.
Visitors to Mother House kept arriving but had to wait outside until the morning prayers finished at about 7 a.m.
"We came to seek Mother's blessings," said Chaya Das, 60, who lives nearby and had brought her 16-year-old daughter, Arti.
"My daughter is preparing for her examinations," Das said. "She wanted Mother's blessings."
